time.desc: One side carried out air strikes on the other side's key energy export hubs and its air defense and naval facilities, escalating the conflict and directly affecting its energy export capabilities.

The top leader of one side publicly questioned the status of the top leadership of the opponent and said that he had sent a letter to promote negotiations on nuclear issues. At the same time, the opponent's government responded with an open letter and official statement, saying that it was willing to negotiate but refused to coerce.

One party's top financial officials made public statements on strategic waterway navigation and energy market policies, suggesting that they would not restrict specific ships in the short term but may adjust measures in the future due to the prolongation of the war.
The attacked side confirmed that another core high-level official was killed in the opponent's air strike, becoming one of the highest-level officials to be eliminated since the war began.

The coalition launched a new round of attacks on its opponents' super-large gas fields and other energy infrastructure, and there were signs of the substantial closure of the strategic waterway and the spillover effects of production cuts.

The top leader of one party issued a time-limited ultimatum, requiring the opponent to restore commercial navigation of the strategic waterway, otherwise it will turn to attack the opponent's key civilian infrastructure such as electricity.

The rival military has publicly warned that it will take escalating countermeasures if its energy facilities are attacked, including comprehensive closure of strategic waterways and threats of economic countermeasures.
One party announced that it had entered into dialogue with its opponent and temporarily suspended attacks on its energy facilities for several days to create a window for negotiations.
One party formally submitted a multi-clause conflict-ending plan to its opponent in an attempt to push the ceasefire framework into the textual game stage.

The opponent completed a formal written response to the multi-term ceasefire plan, bringing the negotiation to a new stage. However, at the same time, the "beheading" of key military command levels made the situation more uncertain.
The two parties carried out joint attacks on key terminals close to strategic waterways and caused casualties, indicating that attacks around sea lanes continue.

Major forces outside the region have jointly proposed a new multi-point plan for ceasefire and restoration of strategic waterway traffic, forming an alternative mediation path that is different from the text of the warring parties.
The leader of the attacking party publicly called on all countries to go to the key straits to rush for oil, claiming that the attacked party had basically been defeated.

In a nationally televised speech, the top leader of one side announced that he would impose harsher attacks on his opponents within weeks and reiterated a timetable for ending the conflict, signaling an escalation.

The two sides carried out joint air strikes on their opponents' important petrochemical industrial parks and facilities around export ports, continuing to reduce their energy industry production capacity.

The two sides escalated threats to each other through social media: one side named its opponent's power and transportation hubs, while the other warned that it might extend the blockade to another key waterway.
One side agreed to suspend bombings and attacks against its opponents for about two weeks, forming a clear ceasefire window and triggering a rapid fall in energy market risk premiums.

There are public disagreements over the scope of the ceasefire: allies on one side say it does not cover their actions on third-party fronts, while the other side urges that the front be included in the ceasefire.

One navy officially launched a naval blockade against its opponent and declared that it would not affect the navigation of non-opponent ports, significantly changing the prospects for ceasefire and navigation.
